title: Games That Travel
bigQuestion: How does a game move from one town to the whole world?

story.title: A Ball With No Writing
story.kicker: A worn ball in a closet carries the marks of many hands.
paragraphs: A brown ball sits on a closet shelf. It has no name printed on it. Its skin is scuffed and soft. Many hands have thrown it and kicked it.
Balls are very old. Long ago, people in Mexico played with balls made of rubber. Rubber comes from the sap of a tree. Those balls bounced high.
Later, games began to travel far. Soccer rules left London on paper in 1863. Basketball left a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, after 1891.
Teachers, sailors and students carried the games. They took a ball. They also took the rules. Soon, children in many countries played the same games.
story.think: If you moved to a new town, what game would you bring with you?

lessons.title: Rubber Balls in Mexico
lessons.mainIdea: People in Mexico and Central America played ball games with rubber balls long ago.
reading: Long ago, people in Mexico and Central America made *rubber* balls. They got the rubber from the sap of trees. The balls were heavy and bouncy.
They built long ball *courts* out of stone. The courts had high walls on two sides. You can still visit old stone courts there today.

words.d: a stretchy, bouncy stuff made from the sap of some trees
a flat place with edges, made for playing a game

look.title: Picture an Old Court
look.text: Look at a long, narrow floor made of stone. Tall stone walls stand on both sides. The sun is hot. A heavy rubber ball rests in the middle.
look.prompt: What tells you this place was made for a game?

check.q: What were the old balls in Mexico made of?
check.why: People in Mexico and Central America made balls from rubber tree sap.

check.q: Where does rubber come from?
check.why: Rubber is made from the sap of some trees.

check.q: What were the old ball courts built from?
check.why: The old courts in Mexico and Central America were built of stone.

lessons.title: Soccer Rules in London
lessons.mainIdea: In 1863, clubs in London wrote down one set of soccer rules.
reading: In England, towns and schools kicked balls in many ways. Each place had its own rules. Teams from two places often argued.
In 1863, clubs met in London. They made the Football *Association*. They wrote one set of rules, called the Laws of the Game. Now far-away teams could play together.

words.d: a group of clubs that agree to work together
words that tell everyone how a game works

look.title: One Book of Rules
look.text: In 1863 the Football Association in London printed one short list of laws. Any club that joined agreed to play by the same list.
look.cite: The Football Association, Laws of the Game, 1863
look.prompt: Why does it help when two teams use the same list?

check.q: Where did the Football Association begin?
check.why: Clubs made the Football Association in London.

check.q: When did the Football Association begin?
check.why: The Football Association began in 1863.

check.q: What is an association?
choices: a group of clubs that work together
check.why: An association is a group of clubs that agree to work together.

lessons.title: Sailors and Workers
lessons.mainIdea: Sailors, workers and students carried soccer to new countries.
reading: In the late 1800s, British ships sailed to many ports. Sailors played soccer when they landed. Workers and students from Britain played in new lands too.
People in those lands joined in. They started their own soccer *clubs*. Soon the game belonged to them, not only to Britain.

words.d: a group of people who meet to play a game together

look.title: Picture a Port
look.text: Look at a big ship tied up at a dock. Sailors walk down to a sandy lot. One sailor carries a ball. Children from the town stand and watch.
look.prompt: How might the children learn the game?

check.q: Who helped carry soccer to new countries?
check.why: Sailors, workers and students from Britain played soccer abroad.

check.q: What did people in new lands start?
check.why: People in new lands started their own soccer clubs.

check.q: When did soccer spread by ship?
check.why: Soccer spread by ship in the late 1800s.

lessons.title: FIFA Starts in Paris
lessons.mainIdea: FIFA began in Paris on May 21, 1904, to link soccer groups from many countries.
reading: By 1900, many countries had soccer groups. They wanted to play each other. So on May 21, 1904, leaders met in Paris.
They made *FIFA*. FIFA links the soccer groups of many countries. Seven countries in Europe started it. In 1930, FIFA held the first World Cup in Uruguay.

words.d: the world group for soccer, started in Paris in 1904
a soccer contest between countries, first held in 1930

lessons.title: A Winter Game Travels
lessons.mainIdea: YMCA teachers carried basketball from Springfield to gyms far away.
reading: In 1891, James Naismith taught at a *YMCA* school in Springfield, Massachusetts. He made up basketball for a cold winter gym. The first goals were peach baskets.
His students were learning to be YMCA teachers. They moved to YMCA gyms in other towns and countries. They took the new game with them.

words.d: a group with gyms and clubs in many towns; it trained gym teachers

look.title: Picture a Winter Gym
look.text: Look at a gym with a wooden floor. Snow falls outside the window. A peach basket hangs high on the balcony rail. A ball waits on the floor.

check.why: James Naismith made up basketball in Springfield in 1891.

check.why: The first goals were peach baskets.

check.q: How did basketball reach other towns?
check.why: Naismith's students became YMCA teachers and took the game to other gyms.

lessons.title: Basketball at the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: Men's basketball joined the Olympics in 1936, and women's basketball joined in 1976.
reading: The *Olympics* are games where countries meet. In 1936, men's basketball joined the Olympics in Berlin, Germany. James Naismith went to watch.
The 1936 games were played outside on courts of dirt and sand. Women's basketball joined the Olympics later, in 1976, in Montreal, Canada.

words.d: big games where people from many countries compete

check.why: Women's basketball joined the Olympics in 1976, in Montreal.

lessons.title: A Hall in Springfield
lessons.mainIdea: The Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame stands in Springfield, Massachusetts.
reading: Basketball began in Springfield. Today a big *museum* stands in that city. It is the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame.
A *hall of fame* honors great players, coaches and teams. It keeps old balls, shoes and photos. Visitors come from many countries to see them.

words.d: a building that keeps old things so people can see them
a place that honors people who did great things in a field

look.prompt: What could this old ball teach you about the past?
